Macro pulse: The Australian dollar can't catch a break, even with inflation running hot
body: You know it's a tough market out there when even an inflation scare can't buy the aussie a decent day in the sun.

The currency got a bit of a lift earlier today amid a hotter-than-expected October inflation report in Australia. The report showed trimmed mean inflation jumping to 3.8% in October, up from 3.6% in the month before. That saw AUD/USD climb up to a high of 0.6660 on the initial reaction but the pair is now down 1.1% on the day to 0.6560. Woosh.

As much as the inflation numbers make for another compelling argument to the higher for longer narrative, the RBA has already explicitly signalled its preference to pause and assess things after raising the cash rate to 4.85% earlier this month.

And if you look at cash rate futures, there hasn't been any meaningful shift in RBA pricing even after the data today. Traders are still anticipating no change in December and February next year, with roughly 97% odds of the central bank staying pat next month.

That aside, just keep in mind that the monthly CPI numbers typically don't carry quite as much weight as the quarterly inflation report in shaping the RBA outlook. As such, I'd circle the release of the Q4 inflation numbers in January as the much bigger test of the central bank's resolve.
In the meantime though, the aussie has a bigger problem on its hands.

The resumption in the equities selloff this week alongside renewed tariff worries are hardly conducive to buying a currency that thrives on global risk appetite. US futures are seeing losses deepen again today with S&P 500 futures now down 1.5% and Nasdaq futures down 2.4% after stumbling yesterday. All of a sudden, the Monday bounce looks like a fever dream.
And the rush dollars is only intensifying the risk backdrop this week with traders running out of places to seek shelter.

Now, I wouldn't rule out another potential RBA rate hike down the road but what good is a relatively attractive interest rate when investors are more concerned about preserving capital than chasing returns in the immediate term?

At this juncture, it's all about what the market is focusing on and emphasising more. And right now, the aussie has more to gain from a convincing turnaround in Wall Street than another hot monthly inflation print. But unfortunately, we're not quite there yet.

news.title: Market playbook: Where do investors hide when stocks, gold and Bitcoin are all struggling?
body: When everything seems to be on fire, where does one go to hide? Stocks are struggling, gold isn't offering much shelter and Bitcoin is hardly living up to its billing as digital gold. Even the bond market isn't exactly welcoming as of late, even though we are seeing yields come off the boil in the past week.
At this juncture, you'd be forgiven for thinking that stuffing money under the mattress is starting to look like a half-decent investment strategy.

Jokes aside though, diversification might sound great on paper. However, what happens when the things you own for entirely different reasons all start moving in the same direction? Now, that's a real problem.

Higher bond yields, persistent inflation worries and a scramble for liquidity can create precisely that sort of headache. And when investors need to raise cash or when they are forced to reduce leverage, they don't necessarily sell what they dislike. Sometimes, they simply sell what they can.
So, where should one be looking in this sort of market environment?

Always remember this. Holding on to cash is a position too. Often times, investors underestimate the value of simply sitting on their hands when it comes to trading. The idea of not losing money i.e. capital preservation can at times be a better one than bleeding your account balance dry.

Besides, there is also the fact that cash and money market funds offer some potential interest income. However, the most important thing is that they offer the flexibility to buy when more attractive opportunities present themselves.

Then, there are also short-duration bonds. If you're worried about yields continuing to climb, locking yourself into long-dated bonds carries considerable interest rate risk. As such, short-term government bills allow you to collect income with less exposure to those swings, although returns could fall as interest rates come down. However, accessing these are not as simple especially for a retail trader.

For those who still want equity exposure, there's always defensive stocks - particularly consumer staples and healthcare companies with healthy balance sheets and reliable cash flows. When financial troubles hit, people might postpone upgrading their phones but they're not going to stop buying toothpaste. That being said, just be mindful that defensive businesses don't necessarily make for defensive investments if you're overpaying for them. So, there's that to consider.
But perhaps the bigger challenge these days is resisting the urge to do something.

If you pick up your phone and spend ten minutes doom scrolling through social media, you'll probably find someone calling whatever is happening now a generational buying opportunity, someone predicting financial armageddon and someone showing off how much money they supposedly made trading both.

It's remarkably easy to let someone else's conviction become your own, especially when markets are moving violently. If anything, it goes to show FOMO isn't exclusive to bull markets. It can be just as dangerous, if not even more so, when you're desperately trying to catch the bottom.

There's value to the advise of being late to the party than trying to be the one to catch the falling knife. I'd much rather miss the first 5% of a recovery than buy something purely because I'm afraid of being left behind.

After years of being rewarded for buying the dip, perhaps we need to remind ourselves that capital preservation is a perfectly respectable investment objective too. Come what may, there's no medal for being fully invested at every waking hour of every day. Sometimes, the best trade is simply making sure that you have enough ammunition left for the next big opportunity that comes along.

news.title: Gold erases gains as Nvidia optimism fades and US moves to restore tariffs to 2025 levels
body: Gold erased all the weekly gains yesterday as the market optimism from Nvidia news faded rather quickly. The catalyst seemed to be the WSJ report saying that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and other countries as early as this week.

After the Supreme Court ruling, the Trump administration has been attempting to recreate a similar tariff structure through a different legal route, with country-specific investigations providing the justification.

This basically means that the Supreme Court ruling might have temporarily disrupted the tariff agenda without producing a lasting reduction in the effective tariff burden. So, we are going back to broadly similar levels to those imposed in 2025.

According to the Financial Times, the US is expected to honour previous trade agreements by capping the new tariffs for countries that had negotiated deals with the Trump administration. Overall, this isn’t a major gamechanger, but it still adds to inflation and growth concerns.

For gold, it’s a tricky situation because it keeps getting smashed lower when the stock market falls on growth concerns and the gains are capped when the sentiment improves because the US dollar and real yields get support from the hawkish repricing.

Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war. But buyers will also need to be aware that a dovish repricing from renewed stock market selloff could lead to more liquidations.

On the daily chart, we can see that gold (CFD contract) erased the recent gains and it’s now approaching the key 3,500 level again. We can expect the buyers to step in around the 3,500 level, with a defined risk below it, to position for a rally into the downward trendline. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to target the 3,100 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a downward trendline defining the bearish momentum. We can expect the sellers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next.

On the 1 hour chart, the support zone around the 3,600 level turned into resistance now. If we get a bounce from the 3,500 level, we can expect the sellers to step in around the resistance and the trendline, with a defined risk above the trendline, to position for a drop into new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to increase the bullish bets into the major downward trendline next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.
Today we have the US Core PCE price index and the latest US Jobless Claims figures.

news.title: Gold is losing its grip again as sellers eye a break of the $3,500 level
body: After an early bounce on Monday, gold stumbled in trading yesterday and is down another 1% today and we're already staring at another test of the $3,500 mark. The precious metal is on course for a third straight weekly decline and its sixth in seven weeks. Ouch.
As much as the selling pressures might seem excessive, the fact of the matter is that not much has changed from a technical standpoint this week.

The break below the 100-week moving average (red line) just under $4,000 remains the elephant in the room. That was the first serious breach of the key technical level since 2023 and has disrupted the upside momentum in gold that has helped to sustain the stunning rally for much of the last two years.

As seen with the chart above, what looks to be alarming is that if $3,500 gives way, there isn't much in the way of any major technical support until the $3,000-$3,140 region. That's where the 200-week moving average (blue line) and the 61.8 Fib retracement level of the broader rally come into play. That suggests there is quite a bit of air underneath the current price level.

And as mentioned yesterday, I still like the long-term story for gold. However, there's a difference between liking the asset proposition and liking the trade that is right in front of you. Even if gold is at the cheapest levels for this year, it doesn't mean that it is time to go bargain hunting just yet.

In essence, dip buyers have to prove that they have staying power above $3,500 for an extended period to even be taken seriously at this point. Otherwise, it feels like it is only a matter of time before the next wave of selling hits and we go in search of the next ledge for gold to try and hang on to.
